items.abstract: <jats:p>Road damage detection is essential for supporting efficient road infrastructure inspection, yet conventional visual assessment is time-consuming and may produce inconsistent results when dealing with diverse pavement distress patterns. This study aims to comparatively evaluate YOLOv8s, YOLOv10s, YOLOv11s, and an optimized YOLOv11s configuration for detecting and classifying longitudinal cracks, transverse cracks, alligator cracks, and potholes using the RDD2022 dataset. A quantitative experimental approach was employed using 55,007 annotated damage instances, with all models trained under consistent experimental conditions and evaluated using precision, recall, F1-score, mAP@50, mAP@50–95, and inference time. The results show a progressive improvement across the evaluated configurations, with optimized YOLOv11s achieving the highest performance at 83.4% precision, 80.9% recall, 82.1% F1-score, 88.4% mAP@50, and 59.6% mAP@50–95, with an inference time of 8.7 ms. Class-specific analysis showed that longitudinal cracks achieved the highest F1-score of 85.5%, whereas alligator cracks recorded the lowest at 79.7%, with the largest classification confusion occurring between potholes and alligator cracks. The novelty of this study lies in the systematic cross-generation comparison of YOLOv8s, YOLOv10s, YOLOv11s, and optimized YOLOv11s under consistent experimental conditions while jointly examining overall performance, class-specific behavior, classification errors, and inference efficiency. The study contributes a detailed characterization of model performance across heterogeneous road-damage categories and provides quantitative evidence for selecting an effective YOLO configuration for automated road infrastructure inspection.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:p>As a major and growing global health concern, breast cancer has resulted in a sharp rise of its incidence in India. According to the ICMR estimation, by the year 2023, it has become the cause of almost 27% of all female cancers in India, which is resulting in over 200,000 new cases annually.
 
Time for a diagnosis is the most necessary factor for survival. However, it is often the case that due to the shortage of qualified pathologists and unequal access to healthcare, particularly in the rural areas of India, the diagnosis is delayed. Deep learning (AI) is a technique that can provide a solution to the problem of analyzing medical images in an automated, fast, and accurate manner.
 
Such images include mammograms and histopathology slides. This research paper is a review of the utilization of deep learning models such as CNNs, ResNets, and Vision Transformers for breast cancer cell detection, with a focus on their application in the Indian healthcare context, including datasets, training, performance, and hospital deployment.
 
Further, the paper reviews the real-time implementation and identifies some challenges such as scarcity of data, bias in the model, and integration into the clinical workflow. Finally, it also provides an outline of how AI-based diagnostic systems can contribute to lowering the cancer burden of the country and further improve early detection in underserved areas.</jats:p>
